lead: The physical layer must turn real world phenomena into bits that computers can process. An analog waveform varies continuously in time and amplitude. A digital signal is a sequence of discrete values taken at specific instants. Converting analog to digital (and back) lets us store voice, video and sensor data on binary media and transmit it over cables or wireless links. This conversion is the basis of PCM telephony, audio sampling for music apps, and sensor interfaces in IoT devices.
prereq: You need: basic concepts of signals and systems from Transmission impairments.

blocks.text: An analog signal is a function x(t) that exists for every real time t and can take any value within a range. It is also called a continuous‑time signal. A digital signal is a sequence x[n] defined only at integer indices n and each element belongs to a finite set of symbols. The symbols are often represented by bits (e.g., {0,1}) but may include multiple amplitude levels. A discrete‑time signal is a signal sampled at integer time indices. When the sampled amplitude values are represented by binary symbols, the signal is also a digital signal.

items: Pulse‑code modulation (PCM) is the standard method that creates a digital representation of an analog waveform.

blocks.text: When the sampled amplitudes are encoded as binary symbols, the sampled signal becomes a digital signal.
Only a few universities teach the mathematics of this conversion in depth, but the idea appears in every modern communication system.
Sampling measures the amplitude of an analog signal at regular intervals. If the interval is T seconds, the sampling frequency f_s = 1/T is expressed in samples per second (Hz).

items: Choose a sampling frequency f_s that is at least twice the highest frequency component f_max of the analog signal.

blocks.where: f_s is the sampling rate (Hz); f_max is the maximum frequency present in the analog signal (Hz).

blocks.text: If f_s is lower than 2 f_max the reconstructed signal suffers aliasing – high‑frequency components appear as lower frequencies, corrupting the data.

Quantisation maps each sampled amplitude to the nearest level of a finite set. With B bits per sample there are L = 2^B quantisation levels. The step size Δ (volts) = (V_max – V_min)/L, where V_max and V_min are the allowed voltage range. If V_max and V_min are the extreme quantisation levels, the interval count is L‑1, so Δ = (V_max – V_min)/(L‑1).

blocks.where: L is the number of quantisation levels; B is the number of bits per sample.

blocks.text: Pulse‑code modulation (PCM) concatenates the binary codes of successive samples into a continuous bit stream. The data rate R (bits/s) is R = f_s × B.

blocks.where: R is the PCM bit rate (bits s⁻¹); f_s is the sampling frequency (samples s⁻¹); B is bits per sample.

blocks.code:
f_s = 8000  # Hz
B = 8        # bits per sample
R = f_s * B
print(R)

examples.question: A 1 kHz sinusoid is sampled at 8 kHz and quantised with 8 bits. How many bits are transmitted per second?
steps: Identify the sampling frequency: f_s = 8 kHz = 8000 samples s⁻¹.
Identify bits per sample: B = 8 bits.
Compute the PCM bit rate: R = f_s × B = 8000 × 8 = 64000 bits s⁻¹.
examples.answer: The PCM stream carries 64 000 bits per second.
examples.check:
f_s = 8000
B = 8
R = f_s * B
print(R)

traps: Using a sampling rate lower than twice the highest frequency produces aliasing, which the examiner may ask you to identify.
Confusing the number of quantisation levels L with the number of bits B; remember L = 2^B.
Multiplying the sampling frequency by the number of quantisation levels instead of bits per sample gives a result 256 times too large for an 8‑bit case.
Assuming PCM adds extra framing bits; the basic PCM rate is only f_s × B.

quiz.q: What is another name for a continuous‑time signal?
How many quantisation levels are available with 10 bits per sample?
Explain why the Nyquist criterion f_s ≥ 2 f_max is required for faithful reconstruction.
quiz.a: If f_s is less than twice f_max, higher‑frequency components fold into lower frequencies (aliasing), distorting the reconstructed waveform.

quiz.q: A voice signal contains frequencies up to 3.4 kHz. Choose a suitable sampling rate and compute the PCM bit rate for 8‑bit quantisation.
quiz.a: Choose f_s ≥ 2 × 3.4 kHz = 6.8 kHz; a common choice is 8 kHz. Bit rate R = 8000 × 8 = 64 000 bits s⁻¹.

quiz.q: If a PCM system uses 12‑bit samples at 44.1 kHz, what is the data rate?
Two designers propose different ADC specifications for the same sensor. Designer A: 8‑bit, 8 kHz. Designer B: 12‑bit, 4 kHz. Which provides higher fidelity and why?
quiz.a: Fidelity depends on both resolution and bandwidth. Designer A gives R = 64 kbps, B = 8 bits, f_s = 8 kHz. Designer B gives R = 48 kbps, B = 12 bits, f_s = 4 kHz. Designer B has higher amplitude resolution (12 bits) but lower temporal resolution (half the sampling rate). If the signal bandwidth requires >4 kHz, Designer A preserves more detail; otherwise Designer B may be better. The answer should discuss this trade‑off.

quiz.q: What does PCM stand for and what are its three main steps?
quiz.a: Pulse‑code modulation; the steps are sampling, quantisation, and binary encoding.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry PCM is the foundation of digital audio codecs, VoIP, and sensor networks. Research explores oversampling and noise shaping to improve effective resolution without increasing bit depth. Emerging curricula combine PCM with delta‑sigma modulation for low‑power IoT devices. Next you may study how modulation schemes such as QAM build on the PCM bit stream to occupy radio spectrum efficiently.
